article_title: Input structure-driven instability and convergence in large language model clinical reasoning: a formative study using pediatric residency-level MCQs.
citation: Vinson, J., Caronia, C., & Savargaonkar, R. (2026). Input structure–driven instability and convergence in large language model clinical reasoning: a formative study using pediatric residency–level MCQs. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-48326-4
title: Deliver MCQs to LLMs in structured batches of ten to improve reproducibility and reduce cross-model variability
description: This principle recommends administering multiple questions to LLMs sequentially in batches of ten rather than all at once, because the study found batch delivery converged accuracy to 83%–88% with no significant inter-model differences, while simultaneous delivery produced wide dispersion (38%–90%). The batch size of ten was "selected pragmatically to approximate typical USMLE exam pacing (approximately one question per minute) while remaining within context window limits." The article states this "substantially improves LLM response reproducibility and reduces cross-model variability."
requirements: Batch size of ten items, approximating USMLE exam pacing and remaining within model context window limits
constraints: Only a single batch size (ten items) and fixed presentation order were examined; whether smaller or larger batches maintain stability remains unknown
Batch delivery does not eliminate the risk of factual errors; even at 88% accuracy residual errors could have clinical significance
target_learners: medical educators using LLMs as formative learning tools
target_learning_goals: reliable LLM-supported clinical reasoning practice
stable formative assessment
examples: Each model answered the same 77 validated MCQs under all-at-once and batch-of-ten formats, with batch delivery yielding 83%–88% accuracy and a non-significant ANOVA (F(5,456) = 0.294, ρ = 0.916)

title: Institutions should promote balanced digital habits, mental health support, and integrity-centered assessment reform
description: Based on findings that digital behaviors detrimentally affect mental health and ethical conduct, the authors recommend that "findings highlight the need for institutional policies that promote balanced digital habits, mental health support, and integrity-centered assessment reforms in Ghanaian tertiary institutions." citation: Pilakouta, M. (2008). Statistical uncertainty in educational experiment on the attenuation of gamma radiation. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Background subtraction and decreasing net counts raise the relative statistical uncertainty in low-statistic counting measurements
description: The paper derives, in an appendix, how background radiation affects the relative statistical uncertainty of net counts: Nnet = Ns − Nb with combined uncertainty σnet = √(σs² + σb²). It shows that "Due to the propagation of errors the background subtraction increases the statistical uncertainty of each measurement", and that as net counts fall with absorber thickness the relative uncertainty grows further. For attenuation to half intensity (α=2), Equation (2) indicates the relative statistical uncertainty "increases at least 1.4 times in comparison to the relative uncertainty of the measurement without absorber". requirements: Knowledge of the background counting rate and the source counting rate, obtained before the main measurements, is needed to estimate the uncertainty at the start of the experimental process.
constraints: The exponential attenuation law and this uncertainty analysis apply under narrow-beam, monoenergetic point-source conditions with background accounted for; the analysis concerns low count rate and limited measurement time.
target_learners: non-physics-major undergraduate students in introductory physics laboratories
target_learning_goals: understanding statistical uncertainty of counting measurements
understanding the role of background radiation in measurement uncertainty
examples: In the TEI Piraeus setup, about 84 counts/min gross, 14 counts/min background, and 4-minute measurements give about 280 initial net counts with roughly 6% relative uncertainty, rising to about 12% near maximum absorber thickness.

Inference uses a data augmentation strategy with the location-scale mixture representation of the Asymmetric Laplace distribution, yielding straightforward Gibbs sampling with conjugate normal priors and posterior credible intervals. The model is estimated with the R package bayesQR and compared against a Bayesian logistic regression.

Normalized slope parameters (Euclidean norm) to compare coefficients across quantile levels, since the BQR parameter vector is identified only up to a scale
constraints: The regression parameter vector is identified up to a scale, requiring normalization for cross-quantile comparison
Applied here to a single institution's administrative data; the authors note a multilevel extension for nested university structures should be developed

target_learning_goals: Understanding and predicting student continuation decisions at the Bachelor-Master transition
examples: The model was applied to 2655 administrative profiles of Bachelor graduates at the School of Economics of Sapienza University of Rome, with quantile levels varied over the grid {0.05,...,0.95} and 10000 post burn-in Gibbs drawings

article_title: A battery-resistor analogy for further insights on measurement uncertainties
citation: Gabriel L. A. de Sousa & George C. Cardoso. (2018). A battery-resistor analogy for further insights on measurement uncertainties. https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.03425v6
title: Battery-resistor-loudspeaker analogy for measurement uncertainty
description: The article proposes a thought experiment in which measurement noise is modeled as a random voltage source in series with an ideal battery, feeding an ideal resistive loudspeaker, so the uncertainty becomes literally audible. In this framework "the acoustic power of the noise is the variance of quantity being measured", while the statistical distribution of the noise corresponds to the timbre of the sound. The circuit lets introductory laboratory students derive the variance as mean noise power, the quadrature addition of uncorrelated uncertainties, and the square-root-of-n scaling of the uncertainty of the mean from basic electric-power arguments rather than advanced statistics.
requirements: Rudimentary concepts of electric power and summation notation, which the article names as the only background knowledge needed to follow the arguments.
constraints: The analogies are directly valid for sums and differences of quantities with uncertainties; propagation through an arbitrary function requires extending the power argument via partial derivatives or finite differences.
target_learning_goals: physical intuition about measurement uncertainties
interpreting standard deviation and uncertainty of the mean
adding uncertainties of uncorrelated quantities
examples: Modeling the sum of two readings as two noisy batteries in series, with a choir versus chatting students as a metaphor for correlated versus uncorrelated noise.
Using the loudspeaker to make the noise power audible, so variance is heard as acoustic power and the noise distribution as timbre.

citation: Robert Belfer, Ekaterina Kochmar, and Iulian Vlad Serban. (2022). Raising Student Completion Rates with Adaptive Curriculum and Contextual Bandits. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.14003
title: Reward shaping for exercise-selection bandits: reward instant success highest and penalize MCQs to preserve free-form practice
description: The article defines a reward function in which more desirable outcomes receive higher rewards: 1.5 for instant success, 1 for eventual success, 0.5 for eventual failure, and 0 for instant and eventual skips. During a grid search the authors "observed that rewarding instant success higher than eventual success led to a higher average completion rate on the dataset". To discourage the model from always presenting multiple-choice questions, the observed reward for MCQs is reduced by 0.4, because free-form questions lead to higher learning outcomes and engagement.
requirements: A defined mapping of interaction outcomes (instant success, eventual success, eventual failure, instant skip, eventual skip) to reward values
A penalty term on MCQ rewards calibrated via grid search
constraints: The reward design was validated in simulation on the historical dataset, not independently in the human trial
target_learning_goals: maximizing exercise completion while preserving free-form question practice
examples: Grid search over reward functions on the simulated dataset showed instant success weighted above eventual success raised average completion rate

process skills such as asking investigable questions and problem solving

citation: Schmucker, R., Pachapurkar, N., Bala, S., Shah, M., & Mitchell, T. (2025). Learning to Optimize Feedback for One Million Students: Insights from Multi-Armed and Contextual Bandits in Large-Scale Online Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00270
title: Multi-armed and contextual bandit formulation of assistance selection in intelligent tutoring systems
description: The article formulates assistance selection as a bandit problem in which each practice question has its own policy over candidate assistance actions. The multi-armed bandit policy selects the action that is "optimal on average across all students", while the contextual bandit framework "personalizes decision-making for students by considering their context features" such as ability estimates and response times. The system learned distinct question-specific policies for 10,210 questions across six science courses.

constraints: Contextual policies can only improve outcomes over MAB policies if the best assistance action varies from one student to another, i.e., the CATE function is sign-changing

target_learning_goals: selecting effective feedback after incorrect answers
improving reattempt correctness and overall practice session performance
examples: The system trained question-specific MAB policies across six science courses and evaluated them offline via 20-times-repeated 5-fold cross validation before live A/B deployment

citation: Lai, S., Choi, J., Kim, J., Kunievsky, N., Potter, Y., & Evans, J. (2026). Biased AI improves human performance but reduces perceived helpfulness. https://osf.io/dgx3w
title: Configure dual AI assistants whose biases bracket the learner's own position to retain performance gains while limiting subjective penalty and one-sided influence
description: The article recommends positioning a human user between two AI assistants holding biases on opposite sides of the user's own view, operationalizing Simmel's tertius gaudens. Acting as an arbiter between equal but opposing voices, users "cast the deciding vote, are always in the majority, attain higher accuracy and feel more empowered". The balanced pair preserved the performance gains of single biased assistance while avoiding its subjective penalty and its exposure to market-misaligned one-sided bias, at no additional conversational cost.
requirements: Two assistants whose biases flank the participant's own perspective
An interface allowing the user to orchestrate exchanges among multiple AIs
constraints: The protection against misaligned advice was structural rather than discerning: when the two assistants' recommendations diverged in quality, participants followed the better one no better than chance (adj. p = 0.890)
target_learning_goals: judgment and decision-making
independent adjudication among competing AI perspectives
examples: In the fact-checking and investment experiments, participants in dual conditions conversed with two assistants in parallel within each turn, each able to see earlier messages but not the other's current response

citation: Wu, Z., Shi, J., Murray, R. C., Rosé, C., & San Andres, M. (2025). LLM Bazaar: A Service Design for Supporting Collaborative Learning with an LLM-Powered Multi-Party Collaboration Infrastructure. CSCL 2025 Proceedings. http://bit.ly/4leDl0U
title: Bazaar's distributed listener-actor-output-coordinator architecture for dynamic collaboration support
description: Bazaar manages the complexity of supporting collaborative groups by distributing support across multiple specialized agents. As the article puts it, the architecture works "by distributing the task of listening for particular events in the collaboration and injecting support of various kinds across multiple specialized agents operating collaboratively in the background". Listeners detect events (rule-based or machine-learned) and place them on a queue; actors propose templated responses with priority and timeout values; an output coordinator selects which response, if any, to emit based on the micro and macro state of the activity and chat. LLM Bazaar extends this by adding LLM agents as listeners and actors.
requirements: Requires an activity plan with subtasks and timing, configured listeners for events of interest, actors proposing responses, and an output coordinator to resolve competing proposals
constraints: The architecture supports dynamic collaboration even without LLM integration; LLM agents only propose responses that the output coordinator may accept or suppress
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement in collaborative discussion
academically productive talk such as elaboration, challenge, or explanation
examples: In the regex activity, one agent manages conversation flow, another maintains student engagement, and a third provides targeted hints.

citation: Ett, B., Le Roux, B., Delserieys, A. (2026). Sensemaking in Sound from a Free-Response Final Exam for 6th Grade Physics. J Theor Exp Appl Phys, 2(3), 01-17. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/3070-6505
title: Two levels of sensemaking (Basic and Advanced) for lower secondary physics, related to Bloom's Taxonomy
description: The article defines two levels of sensemaking for assessing sixth-grade physics understanding: "student responses were divided according to their understandings of specific topics into two categories which we define as the two levels of sensemaking: Basic and Advanced, related to and based upon the first three levels of Bloom's Taxonomy." The Basic level encompasses memorization, restating facts, definitions, formulas, and a materialistic view of sound as a physical thing; the Advanced level incorporates outside knowledge, discusses processes and connections among multiple topics, and treats sound as a process and a form of energy. The Basic level aligns with "Remembering" in the revised taxonomy, while Advanced aligns with "Understanding" and touches on "Applying."
requirements: Applied to a topic with rich direct physical experience and sufficient student discussion depth, as the article chose sound for this reason
constraints: For 6th grade students only the first two levels of Bloom's taxonomy are deemed appropriate; the authors note expectations would encompass more levels at higher grades
Physics-specific taxonomies have only been constructed at the university level, not lower secondary
target_learning_goals: Physics conceptual understanding and sensemaking, particularly of sound and waves
examples: The authors applied the levels to three representative students' sound responses: Student 2 (mostly Basic with Advanced indicators), Student 9 (fully Basic with traces of Advanced), and Student 17 (Advanced).

title: Barrier-to-design backward mapping from documented PER barriers to learning goals, activity prompts, and rubric evidence
description: The module is organized around six recurrent learner barriers drawn from physics education research: superposition as physical splitting, basis-change errors, coherent-superposition/mixture conflation, finite-sample misconceptions, ordered-operation reasoning, and notation ambiguity. "Documented barriers determine the learning goals, which in turn determine the activity prompts and assessment evidence." Table I makes the alignment explicit, and the article argues the structure is portable: instructors adapting it for another topic can identify barriers from the literature, state the design response as a prompt, and specify which assessment item evidences each goal.

constraints: Barriers requiring density matrices, multi-qubit entanglement, or full Hamiltonian time evolution were excluded as outside the scope of a single class meeting

predict basis-dependent measurement probabilities
interpret finite-sample variability without state change
communicate reasoning in consistent Dirac notation

citation: Cheng-Han Yu and Angela Ebeling. (2026). Active Learning with Bayesian Reasoning: A POGIL-Based Pedagogy in Introductory Statistics. arXiv:2606.08660. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08660
title: Reproducible Bayesian bivariate generalized linear modeling framework for evaluating instructional innovations
description: The article provides a transparent analytic framework pairing outcome-appropriate likelihoods in a Bayesian bivariate generalized linear model: "Bayes' theorem exam scores were modeled with a zero–one inflated Beta distribution because the scores were bounded between 0 and 100 and included many perfect scores," while satisfaction used a cumulative logit formulation with three ordered levels. Both submodels shared predictors (instructional style, major type, gender, race), used weakly regularizing priors, and were fit in brms with Stan, reporting posterior means and 95% credible intervals. Deidentified data, analysis code, and instructional materials are archived in an Open Science Framework repository.
requirements: Outcome-specific likelihoods matched to scale and distribution (zero–one inflated Beta for bounded scores with a point mass at perfect scores; cumulative logit for ordinal satisfaction)
Weakly regularizing priors and posterior predictive checks for model adequacy
constraints: Interaction models were screened but not retained because they did not improve out-of-sample predictive performance; the framework was applied with a moderate sample size of 94 complete records
target_learners: instructors and education researchers evaluating classroom innovations
target_learning_goals: responsible, uncertainty-quantifying evaluation of instructional interventions
examples: Posterior predictive checks reproduced the concentration of exam scores near 100 and the skew of satisfaction toward the High category, supporting model adequacy

article_title: Modeling Nonlinear Ability Trajectories and Learner Heterogeneity in Online Learning: A Bayesian Nonparametric Dynamic IRT Framework
citation: Zhihua Ma, Alice Xu, Icy Zhang, Guanyu Hu. (2026). Modeling Nonlinear Ability Trajectories and Learner Heterogeneity in Online Learning: A Bayesian Nonparametric Dynamic IRT Framework. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15525
title: Bayesian nonparametric dynamic IRT framework integrating B-spline engagement-drift functions and an MFM prior
description: The framework models binary item responses with a 1PL observation model, tracks within-individual ability across instructional chapters via a first-order Markov state-space process, and specifies expected ability drift through B-spline basis expansions of engagement covariates with cluster-specific scaling coefficients. As the article states, it uses "a dynamic IRT process to track within-individual ability trajectories across instructional chapters, a B-spline basis expansions to capture nonlinear engagement-ability drift, and an MFM prior to infer the number of latent learner clusters jointly with cluster-specific parameters". The MFM prior treats the number of clusters as random, avoiding prespecified K, and the spline specification lets covariate-effect shapes be learned from data. Posterior inference uses tailored MCMC sampling in NIMBLE with ECR relabeling.
requirements: Requires chapter-level engagement covariates and binary item responses across repeated instructional units; the 1PL discrimination constraint was adopted to balance parsimony with the available sample size of 198
constraints: The 1PL formulation constrains item discrimination to unity; the process precision is shared across students, encoding homogeneous temporal smoothness; spline coefficients and cluster scaling coefficients are scale-unidentifiable in isolation, so composite drift is the identifiable evaluation target
target_learners: undergraduate online learners in introductory statistics
target_learning_goals: tracking longitudinal ability trajectories and latent learner profiling to inform adaptive instructional design
examples: Applied to Winter 2023 CourseKata data from 198 undergraduates across 9 chapters and 230 dichotomous items, with two standardized engagement quantity measures constructed from platform interaction logs

description: The article frames nurses' pressure ulcer practice through Bandura's social cognitive theory, in which "self‐efficacy refers to one's belief that he/she can successfully perform a certain task, directly affecting behaviour and performance." citation: Brattland Heidi, Holgersen Katrine Høyer, Vogel Patrick A., Anderson Timothy, Ryum Truls. (2022). An apprenticeship model in the training of psychotherapy students. title: Bandura's four-source self-efficacy framework as the proposed mechanism by which psychotherapy apprenticeship raises students' therapy self-efficacy
description: The article draws on Albert Bandura's self-efficacy theory to explain why apprenticeship should work. It states that "Bandura [34] theorized that one's self-efficacy in a given area is influenced by four sources: Mastery experiences of being able to succeed in performing behaviors or tasks in that area, vicarious experiences of watching social role models similar to oneself perform such behaviors or tasks successfully, verbal persuasion in the form of positive feedback and encouragement from others, and one's own level of emotional arousal while performing the task." Apprenticeship maps onto all four: performing simple in-session tasks builds mastery, observing relatable therapist role models provides vicarious experience, therapist feedback is verbal persuasion, and repeated exposure to real therapy may reduce arousal. Higher self-efficacy is expected to help students approach tasks flexibly, cope adaptively, and persist.
requirements: Exposure to relatable therapist role models performing therapy in a real-life setting
Opportunities for students to perform simple psychotherapy tasks in session
constraints: The mechanism is a theoretical expectation stated by the authors, not a tested result in this protocol
target_learners: First-year clinical psychology students with high worry about their therapy abilities
target_learning_goals: Increase beliefs in one's ability to perform psychotherapy successfully
Decrease performance anxiety and stress in treatment sessions
examples: Students can perform simple tasks such as expressing warmth and positive regard, sharing their understanding of the patient, and history-taking, thereby gaining mastery experiences
key_sources: Brattland Heidi, Holgersen Katrine Høyer, Vogel Patrick A., Anderson Timothy, Ryum Truls. (2022). An apprenticeship model in the training of psychotherapy students. Study protocol for a randomized controlled trial and qualitative investigation. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0272164

article_title: Novel ways to explore surgical interventions in randomised controlled trials: applying case study methodology in the operating theatre.
citation: Blencowe Natalie S., Blazeby Jane M., Donovan Jenny L., Mills Nicola. (2015). Novel ways to explore surgical interventions in randomised controlled trials: applying case study methodology in the operating theatre. Trials. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13063-015-1127-x
title: Balance adequate standardisation of surgical interventions against pragmatism, using minimum standards rather than strict standardisation
description: The article argues that the degree of standardisation should be driven by the research question and trial design, and that strict standardisation may reduce generalisability and surgeon buy-in. A balance between adequate standardisation and practicality is necessary; one approach is to standardise key functions rather than specific forms, or to determine the minimum active ingredients and the degree to which they need standardising. Surgeons in the study considered that "some 'minimum standards' might be important in ensuring that procedures were performed in broadly similar ways."
requirements: Agreement among trial surgeons and, ideally, the wider surgical community on the boundaries within which intervention components are delivered
constraints: In pragmatic multi-centre trials with large numbers of surgeons, specifying each operative step is likely to create difficulties and ensuring each step was delivered as planned may be unrealistic
target_learning_goals: describe and standardise surgical interventions appropriately within trial protocols
examples: Surgeons in the By-Band pilot described ground rules keeping procedures similar without being grossly dissimilar, balancing pragmatism with rigidity

article_title: Learning the Curriculum with Bayesian Optimization for Task-Specific Word Representation Learning
citation: Yulia Tsvetkov, Manaal Faruqui, Wang Ling, Brian MacWhinney, Chris Dyer. (2016). Learning the Curriculum with Bayesian Optimization for Task-Specific Word Representation Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.03852
title: Bayesian-optimization framework for curriculum learning with diversity, simplicity, and prototypicality feature groups
description: The article formulates curriculum learning as an optimization problem: paragraphs are scored by a linear function w⊺φ(X) over linguistic features, sorted by score to define the training order, and the weights are tuned by Bayesian optimization (EI acquisition, TPE surrogate) to maximize downstream task performance. It defines "three groups of features aimed at analyzing statistical and linguistic content and structure of training data: (1) diversity, (2) simplicity, and (3) prototypicality", drawing on prototype theory and second-language acquisition research. The framework is presented as general and applicable to other models.
requirements: Requires an extrinsic task evaluation metric (eval) on held-out data to serve as the optimization objective, and engineered paragraph-level features φ(X) that are z-normalized across paragraphs.
constraints: The article experiments with optimizing the curriculum of word embeddings; optimization of other models' curricula is proposed only in principle, not demonstrated.
BayesOpt trials were fixed to 10 iterations, matching the shuffled baselines' setup.
target_learners: NLP models trained on large text corpora (Wikipedia)
target_learning_goals: Learning word representations that improve downstream task performance (sentiment analysis, NER, POS tagging, dependency parsing)
examples: The framework optimized curricula for cbow word embeddings trained on 2,532,361 Wikipedia paragraphs, evaluated on four downstream NLP tasks.
key_sources: Yulia Tsvetkov, Manaal Faruqui, Wang Ling, Brian MacWhinney, Chris Dyer. (2016). Learning the Curriculum with Bayesian Optimization for Task-Specific Word Representation Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.03852

article_title: Accurate Radar Measurements of Drag Coefficients in Free Flight
citation: Elya Courtney, Collin Morris, and Michael Courtney. (2016). Accurate Radar Measurements of Drag Coefficients in Free Flight. The Physics Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1119/1.5064562
title: Undergraduate lab design should balance simplicity, sufficient accuracy to avoid ascribing discrepancies to confounding factors, and student attention
description: The article opens with a three-factor design principle for undergraduate labs: experiments should be simple and connected with learning objectives, sufficiently accurate that theory–measurement comparisons do not leave gaps students fill with confounding factors such as imperfect simplifying assumptions, measurement uncertainties, and "human error", and engaging enough to ensure due diligence in execution and analysis. The Airsoft radar lab is offered as a design meeting these demands.
requirements: Experiments must be sufficiently accurate for comparisons between theory and measurements without gaps when students ascribe discrepancies to confounding factors
target_learning_goals: connecting theory and measurement in experimental labs
due diligence in execution and analysis
examples: The drag-coefficient lab is presented as achieving near 1% accuracy with affordable equipment, addressing the accuracy factor

article_title: Towards the Baikal Open Laboratory in Astroparticle Physics
citation: Pavel Bezyazeekov, Igor Bychkov, Nikolay Budnev, Daria Chernykh, Yulia Kazarina, Dmitriy Kostunin, Alexander Kryukov, Roman Monkhoev, Alexey Shigarov, and Dmitriy Shipilov. (2021). Towards the Baikal Open Laboratory in Astroparticle Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.10594
title: The Baikal Open Laboratory concept: an open-science education and instrument-development testbed for multimessenger astronomy
description: The Baikal Open Laboratory is a proposed educational and outreach unit focused on multimessenger astronomy and open science, resting on three pillars: development of open training programs, focus on modern IT and open-source solutions, and interaction between different facilities. It exploits the co-location of Irkutsk State University with the TAIGA gamma observatory and the Baikal-GVD neutrino telescope, which the authors call a unique environment "on-site". The neighborhood of experiments measuring different messengers and the large educational center naturally lead to the Baikal Multimessenger concept, a testbed for future multimessenger activity.
requirements: Cooperation with the TAIGA and Baikal-GVD facilities
informational support from the GRADLCI framework and the astroparticle.online platform
educational resources at ISU including its international schools
constraints: Data transfer between experiments can be complicated by data policies established by the different collaborations
target_learners: university students in particle and astroparticle physics
future experts in big data and deep learning for physics analysis
target_learning_goals: training experts in astroparticle physics and multimessenger astronomy
developing methods and techniques for multimessenger astronomy
examples: The laboratory's objectives include training experts, developing new instruments and methods for multimessenger astronomy, and supporting open software and open data initiatives

article_title: How about that Bayes: Bayesian techniques and the simple pendulum
citation: Matthew Heffernan. (2022). How about that Bayes: Bayesian techniques and the simple pendulum. https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08621
title: A five-step Bayesian modeling workflow for teaching-laboratory data analysis
description: The article presents a reproducible Bayesian inference workflow progressing "from explicitly deﬁning prior knowledge all the way to verifying that the ﬁnal inference reproduces expectations". Its steps are: (1) defining a motivated prior, (2) prior predictive checks, (3) model validation via closure testing with pseudodata, (4) inference with real data, and (5) posterior predictive checks, followed by Bayesian model selection with the Bayes factor. Each step is described, motivated, and implemented before progressing to the next, and the workflow is offered as a general introduction to Bayesian techniques for the undergraduate physics curriculum.
requirements: A well-designed step-by-step workflow so analysis can be broken into digestible, concrete steps and troubleshooting is straightforward
Priors that are constraining but do not pre-determine or bias the result, since a prior that precludes the true result can never recover it
constraints: Generalizing the variance propagation to higher dimensions is beyond the scope of this work
Only one parameter, g, is varied in the inference
target_learners: undergraduate physics students in introductory teaching laboratories
target_learning_goals: Bayesian statistical modeling and model selection
systematic data analysis and model-to-data comparison in physics laboratories
examples: The workflow is demonstrated end-to-end on the simple pendulum: inverse gamma prior on g, prior predictive checks, closure testing with pseudodata, inference on real photodiode measurements, posterior predictive checks, and Bayes-factor model selection
key_sources: Matthew Heffernan. (2022). How about that Bayes: Bayesian techniques and the simple pendulum. https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08621

article_title: Task diversity produces systematic transfer but inhibits continual reinforcement learning
citation: Purab Seth, Neil Shah, Ishaan Sinha, Kunal Jha, Samuel J. Gershman, Max Kleiman-Weiner, Wilka Carvalho. (2026). Task diversity produces systematic transfer but inhibits continual reinforcement learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00880
title: Banyan: a GPU-accelerated continual RL domain with three independently controllable diversity axes
description: Banyan is a MiniGrid-style domain for continual reinforcement learning over compositional task spaces, in which "A task is specified by a task tree and a layout". Tasks decompose into a layout, a task-tree topology, and an object assignment, and procedural generation along each axis independently yields billions of compositional tasks while preserving control over the amount and source of diversity. The authors release it to enable controlled experiments on how task diversity affects continual RL.
requirements: GPU-accelerated parallel environment stepping to make many-task training practical
constraints: the article states its domains, including Banyan, remain far from real-world settings
target_learning_goals: continual adaptation across sequences of task distribution shifts
compositional transfer of subgoal structure
examples: the authors co-varied layout and topology diversity from n=1 to n=256 across ten task distributions in Banyan

article_title: Through Einstein's Eyes
citation: Antony C. Searle, Craig M. Savage, Paul A. Altin, Francis H. Bennet and Michael R. Hush. (2005). Through Einstein's Eyes. http://www.anu.edu.au/Physics/Savage/TEE/
title: Backlight relativistic raytracer used to render photo-realistic relativistic scenes
description: Backlight is a relativistically-accurate computer graphics code created by a student in 1997 and later rewritten to "allow for objects with different velocities in the same scene". It produced the videos Visualising Special Relativity and Seeing Relativity, the latter "explicitly pedagogic in its design, and featured Einstein's tram". Current development is towards allowing accelerating objects besides the camera and improving the illumination model.
requirements: Computer graphics code that renders scenes under special relativity, including the Lorentz transformation, finite light speed and Doppler shifting
constraints: As of the paper, Backlight does not yet allow accelerating objects other than the camera, and its illumination model was still being improved
target_learning_goals: visualising special relativity
examples: In one four-day Easter weekend the authors went from vague ideas to a working relativistic raytracer

article_title: Effect Size Measure and Analysis of Single Subject Designs
citation: Swaminathan, H., & Rogers, H. J. (2013). Effect size measure and analysis of single subject designs. SREE Spring 2013 Conference.
title: Bayesian MCMC procedure in WINBUGS for posterior inference on single-case treatment effects
description: The article proposes a Bayesian procedure obtaining the posterior distribution of the regression coefficients and the treatment effect parameter. The advantage of this approach is that the posterior distribution contains all the information needed for drawing inferences, and credibility intervals can be constructed without making any distributional assumptions. A Markov-Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) procedure as implemented in WINBUGS is employed for obtaining the Bayesian estimates.
requirements: Computation must be carried out using the MCMC procedure as implemented in WINBUGS
target_learners: researchers conducting statistical analysis of single-subject designs
target_learning_goals: Bayesian inference about intervention effects in single-case research
key_sources: Swaminathan, H., & Rogers, H. J. (2013). Effect size measure and analysis of single subject designs. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563061

article_title: The Family Parenting Influenced Adolescent Brawls Behavior
citation: Heni Nurhaeni, Dinarti, Dwi Priharti. (2016). The Family Parenting Influenced Adolescent Brawls Behavior. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE). http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE
title: Four-type parenting typology (democratic, authoritarian, permissive, neglected) shaping child character
description: The article adopts a typology, attributed to Baumrind, in which "there is a pattern of parenting, namely democratic, authoritarian, permissif and neglected that will affect the formation of the character of a child". It uses this framework to interpret why democratic parenting — open communication, deliberation, togetherness and mutual trust — motivates children toward independence and positive behavior. The article also notes parenting itself is strongly influenced by education, norms/culture, environment, social and economic conditions and family size.
requirements: Parenting operates within family conditions shaped by education, norms/cultural, environmental, social and economic factors and the number of family members, as the article states
target_learners: adolescents aged 15 to over 20 in senior high schools (SMAN and SMK) in Jakarta and Depok, Indonesia
target_learning_goals: character formation
prevention of adolescent brawl and aggressive behavior
examples: The study classified respondents' family parenting and tested its correlation with brawl behavior across intervention and non-intervention high schools
key_sources: Heni Nurhaeni, Dinarti, Dwi Priharti. (2016). The Family Parenting Influenced Adolescent Brawls Behavior. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE). http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE
